'''''Hordeum marinum''''', commonly known as '''sea barley''' or (subspecies ''gussoneanum'') '''Mediterranean barley''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the grass family [[Poaceae]] that grows on bare ground on the shores of Europe and North Africa. It is also found in inland salt flats such as the Pannonian grasslands of Hungary, and it is widely established outside its range in temperate regions of both the north and south hemispheres. It is an annual, producing copious seed when habitat conditions are right, but not persisting in competition with other species. Although it is a relative of an important crop species, it has no uses itself.

==Description==
[[File:Hordeum marinum spike.jpg|thumb|left|A single inflorescence of sea barley]]
Sea barley is an annual with spreading to erect stems that grow to about 40 cm tall. The leaf sheaths are somewhat inflated, relative to the stem size, and can be glabrous or minutely hairy. They have small rounded auricles and a short membranous ligule about 0.5 mm long. The leaf blade is similarly glabrous or hairy, and is up to 4 mm wide.

The inflorescence is a false [[raceme]] up to 5 cm long and laterally compressed, with numerous clusters ("triads") of 3 one-flowered spikelets. Within each triad, the central spikelet is sessile (stalkless) and fertile while the two lateral ones are borne on short pedicels and are barren. Each spikelet consists of a single floret, with a lemma up to 8 mm long and an awn projecting from its tip, up to 22 mm long. On either side of each lemma is a bristle-like glume up to 22 mm long.

Sea barley is wind-pollinated or self-pollinating. The mature spikes become brittle, and break up into small clusters of fruits, which are often dispersed by floodwaters in the winter, or by the movement of livestock. Germination takes place in both the autumn and the spring.<ref name=Cope>{{cite book |last1=Cope |first1=Tom |last2=Gray |first2=Alan |title=Grasses of the British Isles |date=2009 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London |isbn=978-0-901158-420 }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The name ''Hordeum marinum'' was coined by the English botanist [[William Hudson (botanist)|William Hudson]] in his [[iarchive:bub_gb_Jx05AAAAMAAJ/page/56/mode/2up|Flora Anglica]] of 1778, giving as a synonym the pre-Linnean polynomial ''Gramen secalinum maritimum minus'' ("lesser sea meadow-barley"). He gave it the common name "sea barley-grass".

It has few synonyms. [[William Withering]] named it ''Hordeum maritimum'' in 1787, but that name does not stand as Hudson's came earlier.<ref name="powo"/>

Two subspecies of sea barley are recognised. Throughout most of its range ''H. marinum'' ssp. ''marinum'' is the common one, but around the Mediterranean basin ssp. ''gussoneanum'' <small>(Parl.) Thell.</small> (Mediterranean barley) is commoner.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hordeum marinum subsp. gussoneanum (Parl.) Thell. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/8338571 |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name="powo"/> Both are widely established elsewhere in the world. The difference between them is slight: ssp. ''gussonianum'' has a smaller and wingless inner glume to the lateral spikelets, and a more variable chromosome number (2''n'' = 14 or 28).<ref name="Cope"/>

==Identification==
[[File:Hordeum marinum vs secalinum.jpg|thumb|Sea barley (left) and meadow barley are very similar.]]
Sea barley often grows in the same places as [[Hordeum secalinum|meadow barley]] or [[Hordeum murinum|wall barley]]. Meadow barley is perennial, and so will often have tillers, and the leaf sheaths are not inflated. Wall barley has three fertile florets in each triad, and the awns are ciliate (hairy). Both meadow barley and wall barley also have hairy leaf sheaths, whereas sea barley often does not.<ref name="Cope"/><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
Sea barley is native throughout Europe, North Africa and as far east as central Asia. It is also established as an introduction in North and South America, South Africa, Australia and Japan.<ref name=powo>{{Cite web |title=Hordeum marinum Huds. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30066468-2 |access-date=2024-12-26 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> Although it is primarily a coastal plant, it is by no means restricted to seaside areas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hordeum marinum Huds. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/2706053 |access-date=2024-12-26 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref>

Its IUCN threat status, globally, is [[Least-concern species|Least Concern]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Group) |first=Nigel Maxted (Crop Wild Relatives Specialist |last2=expert) |first2=Laura Rhodes (Crop Wild Relatives |last3=Birmingham/CWR) |first3=Isabelle Bradley (University of |date=2014-08-01 |title=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species: Hordeum marinum |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/172273/19410018 |journal=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208054547/https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/172273/19410018 |archive-date=2024-12-08}}</ref> reflecting the fact that it is quite widespread and populations are healthy. In Britain, which is at the northern edge of its range, it is classified as [[Vulnerable species|vulnerable]], because there may have been a decrease in its range in recent decades,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain (Species Status No. 7) {{!}} JNCC Resource Hub |url=https://hub.jncc.gov.uk/assets/cc1e96f8-b105-4dd0-bd87-4a4f60449907 |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=hub.jncc.gov.uk}}</ref> although in fact there has been an increase in the population extent, as measured by the number of occupied grid squares.<ref name=atlas>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.fc6 |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref>

In France its distribution and status follow the same pattern as in Britain: it is mostly restricted to places near the coast, with just casual populations inland. Its status is LC, except in places like [[Picardy]] and [[Pas-de-Calais]] in the north, where it declines to [[Critically Endangered]].<ref name=INPN>{{Cite web |title=Orge maritime |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/102968 |access-date=27 December 2024 |website=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Hordeum marinum Elmley.jpg|thumb|Habitat of sea barley at [[Elmley]] National Nature Reserve, Kent]]
Sea barley grows on patches of bare ground near to the sea, typically along paths or tracks or sometimes in the upper parts of salt marshes. It is also a characteristic plant of the [[Pannonian Steppe|Pannonian]] inland salt grasslands of south-eastern Europe<ref>{{Cite book |last=Polunin |first=Oleg |title=A Guide to the Vegetation of Britain and Europe |last2=Walters |first2=Martin |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1985 |isbn=0-19-217713-3 |location=Oxford}}</ref> and, very occasionally, it is found as a roadside halophyte, many miles from the sea.<ref name=Crawley>{{cite book |last1=Crawley |first1=M.J. |title=The Flora of Berkshire |date=2005 |publisher=Brambleby Books |location=Harpenden |isbn=0-9543347-4-4}}</ref>

It needs a lack of competition from other plants, which is usually created by fluctuating water levels or some form of disturbance, such as trampling and grazing by livestock. It flowers and fruits early in the season (typically in June in northern Europe), and reproduces entirely by seed.<ref name="Cope"/>

In Britain, it is a purely lowland plant, not being found higher than 200 m above sea level.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/altitudes}}</ref><ref name="atlas" />

Sea barley is not recorded in any vegetation community in Britain,<ref name=Rodwell5>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 5: Maritime communities and vegetation of open habitats|year=2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=0-521-39167-9}}</ref> possibly because it was too rare to have been sampled. In Europe, however, it is considered a characteristic species of several EUNIS habitats:
* E6.13 - Mediterranean continental halonitrophilic pioneer communities, which occur on inland mud flats;
* A2.523 - Mediterranean short ''Juncus'', ''Carex'', ''Hordeum'' and ''Trifolium'' saltmeadows, in brackish lagoons on the coast;
* A2.552 - Mediterranean coastal halo-nitrophilous pioneer communities, found on mud flats close to the shore; and
* R6-1 - Mediterranean inland salt steppe, which includes the Pannonian salt flats, where evaporation causes the soils to become saline.<ref name="INPN"/>

There are several fungi that attack sea barley: the smut fungus ''[[Ustilago]] bullata'' produces galls in the flowers, while ''[[Tilletia controversa]]'' creates smut balls in the seeds; meanwhile, several species cause damage to the leaves, including [[Blumeria graminis|barley powdery mildew]], ''[[Puccinia hordei]]'' (including ''P. hordei-murini'' and ''P. hordei-maritimi''), and a fungus called [[Puccinia graminis|stem rust]] is known to infect the culms.

There is also an aphid, ''[[Metopolophium dirhodum]]'' which has been found on sea barley, and a species of thrips, ''[[Limothrips]] angulicornis'', which feeds on the leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hordeum marinum – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/monocots/commelinids/poales/poaceae/pooideae/triticeae/hordeum/hordeum-marinum/ |access-date=2024-12-26 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref>
